transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-15
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Emma Rodriguez (AtlasHealth - Head of ML), Raj Singh (AtlasHealth - SRE), Clara Ng (AtlasHealth - CTO)
Recording id: ff-20261115-8b3c

Summary (auto): quick run through of catalog, demos of compatibility matrix and bench results UI. Customer asks to run a benchmark using 2k clinical notes and wants private deploy options.

[00:00] Maya (Redwood): okay hi everyone, thanks for joining, uh we can do intros quick — I'm Maya, AE on this account, and Jordan is our solutions engineer who will walk through the catalog+bench flow.
[00:22] Emma (AtlasHealth): hi thanks, Emma here. we've got Raj and Clara — we're primarily interested in inference cost on these clinical summarization flows and whether we should run hosted first or go straight to a private dedicated pool.
[00:45] Jordan (Redwood): great, thanks. quick agenda: catalog filters, compatibility matrix, demo of bench UI in Redwood Console, then Q/A and next steps. sound good?
[01:05] Raj (AtlasHealth): yep, sounds right. also security questions later.
[01:10] Jordan (Redwood): perfect. jumping in — so the model catalog is searchable by model family, architecture, tokenization, and importantly by fit heuristics: we compute latency profiles, quantization sensitivity, and data fit flags from our open-model scouting tests. for ex, we tag models as "medical-tuned?" by looking at eval results and fine tune signals, but that label is fuzzy — sometimes it's misattributed.
[01:40] Emma: when you say fit heuristics, is that based on your public bench runs or you do a lightweight eval per customer?
[01:48] Jordan: it's two parts — a baseline bench in our lab plus a small per-tenant sample run if you want. baseline gives you architecture-level guidance; the per-tenant run uses a handful of representative prompts to estimate quality and latency differences. we recommend the per-tenant bench for clinical data because tokenization quirks matter.
[02:15] Clara: okay, show us the compatibility matrix — I'm curious how you map a model to hardware choices.
[02:22] Jordan: absolutely — switching to the compat matrix view here in Console. we show rows for model variants (e.g., llama2-13b-q4, mosaic-7b-8k, etc) and columns for runtime kernels and hardware — examples: A100-40GB fp16 kernel, H100 sm80-optimized kernel, CPU-avx512 fallback, plus quantized kernels like 4-bit GEMM. cells include expected P50/P95 latencies for a sample 512-token generation, throughput (tokens/sec), and estimated cost per 1k tokens.
[03:05] Maya: note — the kernel mapping is probabilistic because kernel selection can change with sequence length and KV cache hit rate. we show a heatmap: green means strong fit, orange means marginal, red means not recommended.
[03:25] Emma: the heatmap — is that purely performance or does it fold in quality differences after quantization?
[03:32] Jordan: good q. we separate quality and perf. quality delta from baseline fp16 is a separate column; if quantization causes >2% drop on your eval set we flag it. in medical summarization we often avoid the heaviest quant unless the drop is acceptable.
[03:50] Raj: what's the default batching policy? our throughput patterns are spiky around midnight batch jobs and daytime interactive queries.
[03:59] Jordan: Console exposes auto-batching profiles — you can set target latency SLO and the system configures batching/default batch window. for spiky workloads we recommend a dedicated pool with burst capacity configured; for lower QPS hosted with caching and prefix reuse can be more cost-effective.
[04:20] [04:20] Maya (interject): one thing to watch — KV cache hit patterns are huge for cost. if your pipeline sends many repeated prefixes (like patient metadata) caching reduces per-token compute dramatically.
[04:40] Clara: can you run a benchmark that simulates our real prefixes? we'll send a redacted set.
[04:47] Jordan: yes, that's our next step — we can run a contractor bench (pilot) with your samples. we'll do end-to-end: tokens, P50/P95 latency, cost per 1k tokens, and quality delta vs fp16 baseline.
[05:05] Emma: nice. show us the bench UI — what's the input and output?
[05:10] Jordan: here — you upload a prompt/test set, select model candidates, and pick target infra. the results page has an interactive chart: latency distribution, token throughput histograms, and model comparison table. link to example: https://console.redwood.ai/bench/atlas-demo (note: placeholder).
[05:40] [05:40] Speaker 2 (auto): recording paused/resumed (system)
[06:00] Jordan: continuing — we also expose cost knobs: quantization profile, batch size, and kernel hints. you can toggle a "prefetch KV" setting or switch from q4 to q2 quant to see how quality and cost move.
[06:25] Raj: two practical Qs: 1) how long does a per-tenant bench take? 2) can we run it in our VPC?
[06:33] Jordan: typically 24-48 hours to run a proper sample sweep across 6-8 model variants. for VPC/private deploy, we can either run bench on a short-lived dedicated pool inside your VPC (if you want the infra to mirror production) or we run it in hosted infra with encrypted uploads and sign an NDA. for regulated data we'd push for private run.
[06:58] Emma: cost estimate? rough numbers are fine.
[07:03] Maya: ballpark: hosted pilot bench runs range $500–2k depending on total tokens and model set. a dedicated trial to mimic production is higher — mostly dev+infra hours. we'll give precise pricing after we scope the dataset size.
[07:20] Clara: about security: do you have KMS integration and audit logs we can push to our SIEM?
[07:27] Jordan: yes — KMS/HSM integrations exist, we ship audit logs and per-request tracing. SSO via SAML/SCIM and RBAC. we'll send SOC 2 and ISO artifacts — Raj, you'll get network topology docs.
[07:45] Raj: perfect. also, for the compat matrix, can you show memory footprint per model? some of our nodes are memory-constrained.
[07:53] Jordan: yes memory and peak GPU memory are columns in the table — we also show quantized RAM footprint estimates. occasionally the memory estimates are off because of custom kernels but we include a confidence band.
[08:10] Emma: we've been experimenting with two families: flan-ish instruction models and medical-tuned LLMs. which should we prioritize?
[08:18] Jordan: prioritize by quality delta and cost. flan variants often win for instruction adherence at smaller sizes, but domain-tuned models can give edge for hallucination reduction on clinical notes. our playbook recommends building a shortlist of 3: 1 baseline open model (best perf/cost), 1 tuned model, and 1 experimental quantized small model. run A/B evals on your golden prompts.
[08:46] Maya: I'll also add a note: Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization profiles and batching config automatically after initial bench runs. it surfaced a 30% cost win for a health-tech customer by enabling prefix caching + q4 for lower risk prompts.
[09:05] [09:05] Emma: do you support function/tool calling? we're thinking of structured output for EHR extraction.
[09:12] Jordan: yes, function/tool calling is supported at the API level and we have structured output helpers in the SDK. small caveat: with very strict schemas quantization sometimes affects tokenization boundaries — another reason to bench with your schemas.
[09:35] Raj: any competitor concerns — we use HF endpoints for experiments. what's the main reason to select Redwood for serving?
[09:44] Maya: three reasons: production-grade latency controls and fallbacks, unified runtime across hosted/dedicated/private, and tooling that ties bench results to rollout policies and cost metrics. we also have built-in rollback/fallback to smaller models during saturated conditions.
[10:05] Clara: show us a sample canary rollout in Console.
[10:12] Jordan: yeah — in Console you can set a canary percent, tie it to a model version, and set automatic fallback if P95 > threshold or error-rate rises. you can also dot in A/B test results from the bench to seed the canary.
[10:30] Emma: okay, specifics for our POC — we want the bench to include: 2k clinical notes (de-identified), 10 canonical prompts (summaries + extraction), target latency SLO 500 ms p95 for interactive, and batch throughput baseline for nightly jobs.
[10:48] Maya: good, we'll scope that. Jordan, can you take lead on bench plan?
[10:53] Jordan: yep I'll prepare a plan with model shortlist and infra matrix. expected run time 36 hours once we have the dataset.
[11:02] Raj: network question quick — for private deploy, do you use customer-managed keys and is traffic egress blocked?
[11:08] Jordan: yes to both — we can use your KMS, and for on-prem or VPC deploy we do no egress from your network. hosted options do encrypt in transit and at rest and we can add extra constraints.
[11:20] [11:20] Maya (AE): I'll follow up with a checklist: hosted vs dedicated decision guide, pricing ranges, and the bench worksheet.
[11:28] Emma: can we get an ETA on security docs?
[11:31] Maya: I'll send SOC2/ISO and network diagrams by EOD tomorrow.
[11:35] Clara: and please include the compat matrix export so we can review model/hardware mapping offline.
[11:40] Jordan: we can export CSV/PDF from Console. I'll attach the compatibility export to the follow-up email.
[11:47] Emma: great thanks — last q, on cost reporting can we get token-level breakdown per route?
[11:52] Jordan: yep Console cost analytics show token-level, per-route, and per-model breakdowns with traces you can jump into.
[12:00] Maya: ok final recap: Redwood to run bench plan once Atlas sends sample dataset; Redwood to share security artifacts and pricing checklist; schedule POC scoping with Atlas infra next week. action owners noted in the doc. thanks everyone.
[12:15] Clara: thanks all.
[12:18] Raj: thanks.
[12:20] Meeting end.

Notes about transcript quality: automatic transcription had occasional mislabels (Speaker 2) and some technical terms distorted (e.g., "KV cache" transcribed as "kay vee cache" sometimes). We left those as-is to preserve realism.
